A Hopfield memory stores each pattern as a valley in its energy. A damaged letter starts on the valley's side, and Settling rolls it down to the stored pattern.

The pulls record only which pixels agree with which, so the **mirror image** of a stored pattern, with every pixel reversed, is a valley as well: E(-s) = E(s). A settle begun from noise often ends in a mirror or in a fake valley: **22.3%** fake for 5 random patterns.

The letters show the limit of the simplest rule. With the Hebbian rule and the letters S, E, T and L, recall falls into one blend, because the letters overlap and their backgrounds agree. The projection rule makes each letter an exact fixed point.

Each hard location has a fixed random 256-bit address. A write wakes every hard location within the activation radius r of the pattern and adds the pattern to the bit-counters of those hard locations. A read wakes the hard locations near the address and lets them vote, bit by bit. Here there are no mirror images: the bit-counters record the signs of the bits, and they keep no record of how pairs of bits agree.

A soft memory wakes each hard location with a probability that falls smoothly with distance. In the limit its read is a softmax vote over the stored patterns, which is **attention**.

The dial turns the hard cut-off, which wakes a hard location if it lies within the activation radius, into a logistic one. As the cut-off softens, the kernel between two points flattens, and the read becomes a softmax-weighted vote over the stored patterns (Bricken and Pehlevan 2021). The match has a limit: at softness 1 the two reads agree on **99.2%** of bits and both recall 0%, because the matching inverse temperature is too low to pick out one pattern.

A key turns the note before it is stored, so only an address turned by the same key starts near the note's valley. The key hides what the note says. It does not hide that a note is there.

A key is a rotation of the cube: a mask of sign flips together with a shuffle of positions. The note is stored in its turned form, and the holder of the key reads the memory from the turned all-yes padding, which the holder knows. A wrong key turns the result into noise.

A stranger who lands in the note's valley holds the turned pattern, and this reads as about 50% of bits right, which is chance. The key protects the text of the note and leaves its existence visible. It is not cryptography.

## (RECORDED · ACTIVATION RADIUS)

The activation radius decides how many hard locations a read wakes. A very noisy address needs a wider activation radius to reach its pattern, and a wider radius lets the other patterns' noise in.

A small radius keeps a read clean but wakes few locations; a wide one wakes enough locations to reach an address that is far from its pattern, at the price of more noise from the others. The scale test used one activation radius for every address-noise. This test picks the activation radius that keeps an address D x 256 bits away inside the critical distance, and compares it with the SNR radius.

### Capacity against the activation radius, at 10% and 30% address-noise

The 10% peak sits at the SNR activation radius and the 30% peak at the cd0.3 activation radius, plus or minus 1, at every M. No activation radius lifts 40% above 3.

### Capacity stays near 2 at 40% address-noise because whole patterns compete

The stored pattern whose wake set shares the most hard locations with the address wins every bit where it differs.

Every S-map variant treats the other patterns as fresh noise on every bit and predicts about 0.1% failure. The RACE predictor, built after the data, treats them as whole patterns and lands close to the measured failures.

### Reading by content instead of by address

The pulls read wakes a location when its stored counters agree with the current state; the address plays no part. The sealed threshold scaled to the store's density failed, because rows holding one other pattern wake together. Waking exactly the k = p M rows with the largest agreement worked everywhere.

The report scores predictions as right, wrong or split; the site's marks read right as hit and wrong as miss.

## Every memory here carves a valley (HOW THESE MEMORIES WORK)

In Hopfield's memory the patterns are held in the pulls. In Kanerva's sparse distributed memory they are held in the bit-counters of random hard locations, drawn here as lights. The soft version of Kanerva's memory becomes attention in its limit.

## Hard locations and their bit-counters, drawn as lights (LIVE · KANERVA SDM)

This is the memory behind SETTLE’s `sdm` statement. KANERVA parses that statement: the `settle` command mounts KANERVA’s parser as a plug-in, and the `kanerva` command uses the same one, so a line is read one way by both. The KANERVA page shows the word list and the two commands.

## (RECORDED · CAPACITY AND KEYS)

Both memories were filled with random patterns and read from noisy addresses. The tables count how often a read lands on the right pattern.

## (RECORDED · SOFT SDM)

Each bar gives the largest number of stored patterns a memory still recalls at least half the time from a 10% noisy address. A longer bar holds more.

## (RECORDED · SCALE)

Capacity here is P90, the largest stored count at which 90% of reads recall. The chart follows it as the memory grows, and the equations are the prediction we tested it against.

Equations: Bricken and Pehlevan 2021, Eq. 25, as given in the SDMSCALE experiment's report.

## (RECORDED · CODED NOTES)

A note is stored as bits, so fewer bits per character means more text per memory. The tables measure the compression and how many bytes of text come back from each note.
